author: mamadulce69
quote:
**The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time isn’t just the greatest game ever made. It’s the one that made every other contender look like they were still figuring out how to walk.**

Released in 1998 on the Nintendo 64, this game didn’t merely advance the medium—it rewired what players thought a video game could *be*. While other titles were still fumbling with tank controls and flat 2D planes, Ocarina of Time dropped a fully realized 3D world that felt alive, reactive, and mythic. It is the high-water mark. Everything after has been trying (and mostly failing) to catch up.

### Innovation that actually mattered
Z-targeting. That’s it. That single lock-on system—point at an enemy, hold Z, and the camera and combat suddenly make sense—became the foundation for nearly every action game that followed. From Devil May Cry to Dark Souls to modern open-world titles, they all stand on Ocarina’s shoulders. Before this, 3D combat was a clumsy mess. After it, the language of action games was rewritten.

Then there’s the time travel. Child Link and Adult Link aren’t just a gimmick; they’re a structural masterpiece. The same world, seven years later, transformed by your actions (and inactions). The emotional weight of returning to a place you once knew as a child and finding it changed is something most “narrative-driven” games still can’t pull off without cutscenes and exposition dumps. Ocarina did it with pure design.

The ocarina itself? An instrument that is simultaneously puzzle tool, story device, and emotional core. You don’t just press buttons to progress—you *play*. The music isn’t background; it’s language. “Song of Time,” “Saria’s Song,” “Zelda’s Lullaby”—these melodies still hit harder than most modern orchestral scores because they are woven into the act of playing.

### The world still feels bigger than most “open worlds”
Hyrule Field at dusk. The quiet dread of the Lost Woods. The first time you step into the Temple of Time and realize the scope of what you’re about to do. This was 1998 hardware. Cartridge limitations. No seamless streaming. No 4K textures. And yet the sense of place, scale, and discovery remains more potent than many games with a hundred times the budget and polygon count. Modern open worlds are often content checklists dressed in pretty lighting. Ocarina’s world feels authored, purposeful, and alive with secrets.

The dungeons remain some of the best-designed in the medium. Water Temple discourse is eternal for a reason—people still argue about it decades later because it demanded spatial intelligence and patience instead of holding your hand. The game respected the player’s intelligence in a way that feels almost radical now.

### Cultural and critical dominance
It wasn’t just critically adored on release; it became the permanent reference point. Highest-rated game on multiple aggregator lists for years. Frequently ranked #1 in “greatest of all time” polls by outlets, developers, and players who’ve actually played a wide range of games. Its influence is so pervasive that entire genres still borrow its DNA without always acknowledging the source.

And let’s be honest: the emotional high points still work. The reveal of the Master Sword. The adult timeline shift. The final confrontation. The ending that somehow manages to be triumphant, melancholic, and quietly devastating. Most games chase spectacle. Ocarina delivered myth.

### The uncomfortable truth
Plenty of games have better graphics, tighter combat, denser lore, or more “content.” Almost none have the same combination of mechanical invention, emotional resonance, structural elegance, and pure sense of wonder. Many modern titles feel like products optimized for engagement metrics and annual releases. Ocarina of Time feels like someone cared enough to make something permanent.

If you prefer something else, that’s fine. Preferences exist. But claiming any other game sits higher on the pure “greatest ever created” mountain usually requires either nostalgia for a later title, an overvaluation of technical polish, or a misunderstanding of how foundational this one was.

Ocarina of Time didn’t just set the bar. It *became* the bar. Everything else is measured against it—whether people admit it or not.
game_title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (1998)

author: mamadulce69
quote:
This is not a GTA game. This is a $80 monument to corporate cowardice and creative bankruptcy, and the people calling it a masterpiece are either paid, delusional, or so desperate for a new GTA that they’ll orgasm over anything Rockstar dumps on them.**

Thirteen years. A reported billion-dollar budget. The most hyped piece of entertainment in modern history. And what did we get? A glossy, overlong Florida tourist brochure with guns, where the biggest innovation is that the female lead can also commit crimes while the game pretends this is somehow revolutionary feminism instead of the same old blood-soaked sandbox with a new coat of pastel paint.

Lucia and Jason are the most aggressively marketed “complex couple” in gaming history, and their chemistry has all the heat of two wet paper bags dry-humping in a humid alley. The writing keeps insisting their relationship is profound and tragic while every other mission reduces them to interchangeable shooting galleries. Rockstar used to have teeth. Now they have focus-group-approved “representation” and the same tired satire of influencers, cops, and Southern trash that felt edgy in 2013 and just feels exhausted in 2026.

The world is massive, yes. It’s also the most expensive empty shell ever built. NPCs still move like they’re on rails, the AI still has the decision-making capacity ****, and the “living city” mostly consists of background chatter designed to make streamers say “wow the detail” while the actual gameplay loops remain identical to GTA V. Drive. Shoot. Escape. Repeat. The physics still break in embarrassing ways. The frame rate still chokes when too many people are on screen. After more than a decade of development, current-gen hardware still can’t run this thing without compromises. That’s not ambitious. That’s incompetent.

And then there’s the Ultimate Edition scam. You paid the extra money for the “Ultimate” package, right? The one they waved in your face during pre-orders like it was some exclusive paradise of content? Congrats, you’re locked out of half of it until you grind through specific story beats and progress gates. Want that special vehicle, that exclusive outfit pack, those early access bonuses they sold you? Too bad. The game literally holds your paid content hostage until you’ve jumped through the exact narrative hoops Rockstar decided you needed to complete first. It’s not a reward. It’s a leash. They charged you more money and then put a progress wall in front of the very things you already bought. That is pure, unfiltered contempt for the player.

The online is already positioning the single-player as the appetizer so they can milk microtransactions and FOMO events for the next ten years. The same exact playbook that turned GTA Online into a predatory casino with cars. Anyone surprised by this has been living under a rock made of Rockstar’s own marketing.

The people giving this a 10/10 are not reviewing a game. They’re reviewing their own sunk-cost emotional investment. They’re reviewing the trailer they watched fifty times. They’re reviewing the idea of GTA 6, not the thing that actually shipped. The rest of us are stuck with a bloated, safe, self-congratulatory open-world that mistakes scale for substance, nostalgia for progress, and paid content locks for “player engagement.”

Skip it. Wait for the inevitable “definitive” version in three years when they finally fix the performance, unlock the Ultimate Edition content for people who already paid, and add the features that should have been there on day one. Or better yet, go replay something that actually took risks instead of spending another decade polishing the same formula and calling it evolution.
